all.text: Click on a door.

Welcome! This room is filled with thousands of people who answered a question about the afterlife as part of the [Global Flourishing Study](https://globalflourishingstudy.com/). Keep walking!
Scroll to walk
Here’s a mini-map to guide you. Notice how younger people are in the front and older people are in the back.

As you explore, you can click on a person to learn more about them.
Click on a person
As expected, belief in an afterlife is [closely correlated](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-79103-w) to our religious affiliation.
And, of course, it’s correlated with whether they believe in God or gods..
But belief is cheap. That’s why researchers like to hone in on how often they attend religious services.
That said, some people can’t make it to church. So researchers also like to ask how important people say religion is in their lives.
I’ve been bothering you a lot. I’ll let you walk around for a bit.

Scholars long believed that the rise of science knowledge would create an increasingly secular world. But that [hasn’t been the case](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/sacred-and-secular/5CE209CE245D444D40BB44D0DDD78F43).
From the 1980s to mid-2000s, religion exploded—particularly in former Soviet countries, as well as places like China, Mexico, and Brazil. It also rose sharply in the U.S.
But since then, religious belief has fallen in most countries—and the U.S. saw one of sharpest biggest decreases in religious belief.

One theory is that religion enforced pro-fertility norms when infant mortality was high. But those societal needs faded and so did the need for religion. When older generations died, a smaller portion of people were tied to religion .
But then why are there so many people on the right side of this room, believing in the afterlife? Go explore a bit and I’ll be back.
The portion of people who are religious has stayed relatively steady because of two coinciding trends. One is that developed countries became more secular and, in turn, their fertility rates dropped.
The other is that people in developing countries still face existential threats, and religion continues to provide security and predictability. Fertility rates in those countries have stayed high.

There’s one more thing happening: Even though people are less devoted to religion in developed countries, belief in the afterlife has stayed steady—and even increased in some countries, especially among younger people.
We all have to cope with the idea that our natural lives will end—and we can’t help but think about whether there is an existence for us on the other side.

We’ve built stories, rituals, and communities to help us cope with that massive question—and for many of us, knowing that there is something better in the afterlife has helped us cope with the brutal nature of our lives.
But when we encounter people with different stories and rituals, we sometimes [see them as not one of us](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2023.112352). These disagreements have caused great suffering.
Many of us see the people in this room and judge them based on where they are standing right now.

But the amazing part is that, while the unstoppable forces of time push us forward in this room, we are able to walk side to side—change our minds, explore left, right, middle, and everything in between.
In fact, from 2023 to 2024, that’s exactly what a bunch of people did.
Did they end up in the right place? We’ll never know.

You’re among people who do not believe in an afterlife. You heretic! (Just kidding.)
Scroll to walk

To your immediate right are people who are unsure there is an afterlife. On the far right are people who believe in an afterlife.

unsure.text:

Scroll to walk

To your left are people who don’t believe in an afterlife. To your right are people who do believe.
Drag to rotate
